title: Broccoli, fresh, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli is an edible flower head from the Brassicaceae family, originally native to the Mediterranean region. Fresh florets are commonly sautéed in butter or margarine, which preserves their vivid green color and enhances flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli is rich in glucosinolates, compounds that may support the body’s detoxification processes.
It is believed that broccoli was first cultivated in ancient Rome.
Edible parts include not only the florets but also stems, leaves, and even the roots.
Cooking broccoli in butter retains more vitamin C than boiling in water.
In Japan, broccoli is often served as tempura, a light batter made from rice flour.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: One cup of cooked broccoli provides over 100 % of the daily recommended vitamin C, which supports immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Phytochemicals
items.content: Sulforaphane and other glucosinolates have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Cooked broccoli with a modest amount of butter contains about 55 kcal per 100 g, making it a weight‑friendly choice.

items.title: Allergy to cruciferous vegetables
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to broccoli, ranging from itching to gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Broccoli contains raffinose, which can be fermented by gut bacteria and cause flatulence.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Large amounts of raw broccoli may interfere with iodine absorption, which is relevant for individuals on thyroid medication.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté broccoli in butter or margarine over medium heat for 5‑7 minutes until tender yet crisp. Add garlic, lemon juice, or your favorite herbs. Serve as a side dish, in salads, pasta, or baked casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh broccoli in a perforated bag in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C, where it stays fresh for up to 5 days. Cooked broccoli should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge for no more than 3 days. Discard any heads with yellow or slimy spots.
